entries.sentence: A kidney infection, also called pyelonephritis, is a urinary tract infection that affects one or both kidneys.
entries.note: NHS: a type of UTI affecting one or both kidneys

entries.sentence: A kidney infection is a type of urinary tract infection that involves one or both kidneys.
Its main signs are pain in the back or side, nausea and fever, and it is often brought on by cystitis, a bladder infection.
entries.note: NHS: main signs back/side pain, nausea, fever; often caused by cystitis

entries.sentence: It is more common in women, in children, during pregnancy and in older people.
entries.note: NHS causes summary: women affected far more often; also more common in children, pregnancy, older people

entries.sentence: If it is not treated it can lead to sepsis, but most people recover fully when treatment starts promptly.
entries.note: NHS: untreated can lead to sepsis; most make full recovery with prompt treatment

entries.sentence: Bacteria, often Escherichia coli (E. coli), get into the tube that carries urine out of the body.
entries.note: NHS: bacteria often E. coli get into the urethra

entries.sentence: Most kidney infections begin as a bladder infection that spreads upwards to the kidneys.
entries.note: NHS and NIDDK: complication of an ascending UTI

entries.sentence: Less commonly, bacteria reach the kidneys through the bloodstream, and rarely an infection follows surgery.
entries.note: NIDDK: less commonly via bloodstream; rarely after surgery

entries.sentence: Some infections start in the kidney itself, for example when there is a kidney stone or a kidney abnormality.
entries.note: NHS: sometimes due to a problem in the kidney such as stone or abnormality

entries.sentence: Being a woman, because the urethra is shorter.
entries.note: NHS: women affected more often, partly shorter urethra

entries.sentence: Pregnancy, childhood and older age.
entries.note: NHS: more common in children, pregnancy and older people

entries.sentence: A suppressed immune system, for example from cancer or from medicines such as steroids or chemotherapy.
entries.note: NHS: immune suppression e.g. cancer, steroids, chemotherapy

entries.sentence: Poorly controlled diabetes.
A kidney stone or a kidney abnormality.
A blockage such as an enlarged prostate.
entries.note: NIDDK: blockage such as kidney stone or enlarged prostate can cause infection

entries.sentence: Constipation.
entries.note: NIDDK: constipation can increase the chance of bladder or kidney infection

entries.sentence: Fever and chills.
Pain in the side or lower back.
entries.note: NHS symptoms: side or lower back discomfort

entries.sentence: Cloudy urine or blood in the urine.
entries.note: NHS: cloudy urine; blood in urine listed among reasons to seek help

entries.sentence: Confusion in older people.
entries.note: NHS: in older people may cause confusion

entries.sentence: In very young children, a high temperature may be the only sign.
entries.note: NHS/NIDDK: child under 2 may only have high temperature

entries.sentence: Sepsis, which can be life threatening.
entries.note: NHS: untreated can lead to sepsis; NIDDK uncommon but life threatening

entries.sentence: Kidney abscess, which is rare.
Some permanent damage to kidney tissue.
Impaired kidney function or kidney failure.
entries.note: NICE NG111: complications include impaired renal function or renal failure

entries.sentence: Preterm labour in pregnancy.
Clinicians use the history of symptoms, a physical examination, and laboratory and imaging tests.
A urine sample is checked with a dipstick strip for signs of infection and sent to a laboratory, which identifies the bacterium and tests which antibiotics work against it.
entries.note: NHS: dipstick and lab sample; NIDDK: urinalysis and culture

entries.sentence: Blood tests check for serious infection.
Treatment usually starts before the laboratory results return.
entries.note: NHS: treatment usually starts before results; UK guidance: antibiotic prescribed straight away if suspected

entries.sentence: Because kidney infection is much rarer in men, men are routinely investigated further.
Antibiotics are the main treatment, taken by mouth, through a drip into a vein, or both.
Most people are treated at home, while people with a long-term health condition or who are pregnant may need antibiotics through a drip in hospital.
The antibiotic may be changed according to laboratory results, and a blockage such as a stone may need a procedure to clear it.
Paracetamol, rest and plenty of fluids are the usual self-care, whereas anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen are not usually recommended because of possible effects on kidney function.
entries.note: NHS: rest, fluids, paracetamol; ibuprofen not usually recommended; NICE: NSAIDs not recommended, renal safety

entries.sentence: Habits that help keep bacteria out of the bladder and urethra include drinking plenty of plain water, going to the toilet promptly, emptying the bladder after sex and wiping from front to back.
entries.note: NHS prevention summary (search summary of NHS pages)

entries.sentence: Treating constipation also helps.
A GP may prescribe low-dose antibiotics for people who keep getting urine infections.
Call 999 or go to A&E if there is confusion or drowsiness.
entries.note: NHS: call 999 or A&E if confused or drowsy

entries.sentence: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 for a very high or very low temperature, pain in the lower tummy or back, blood in the urine, or pregnancy with these symptoms.
See a GP if a fever comes with pain in the tummy, lower back or genitals that does not go away, and contact a GP straight away if a child may have a kidney infection.
The NHS says kidney infection symptoms usually develop quite quickly, over a few hours or days.
Common signs include discomfort in the side or lower back, fever, chills, tiredness, reduced appetite, nausea and diarrhoea.
Urinary symptoms such as painful peeing, a frequent urge to pass urine and cloudy urine often appear as well.
Clinical references describe a typical pattern of fever, pain in the flank (the side of the back) and nausea or vomiting, although not every person has all of these.
entries.note: StatPearls: classic triad fever, flank pain, nausea/vomiting, not all need be present

entries.sentence: In older people a kidney infection may cause confusion.
Very young children can look different: a child with a kidney infection may have only a high temperature, and may also feed poorly or gain weight poorly.
entries.note: NHS: child under 2 may only have high temperature; NIDDK adds feeding difficulty and poor weight gain

entries.sentence: A kidney infection usually happens when bacteria, often a type called E. coli, get into the urethra, the tube that carries urine out of the body.
In most cases the infection starts in the bladder and spreads upwards to the kidneys, which is why it is often described as a complication of cystitis.
entries.note: NHS and NIDDK: ascending UTI complication

entries.sentence: Less commonly, bacteria reach the kidneys through the blood, and rarely an infection follows an operation.
Sometimes a problem in the kidney itself is behind it, such as a kidney stone or an abnormality of the kidney.
A blockage to the flow of urine, such as a stone or an enlarged prostate, can also be the cause.
Women are affected more often, partly because the urethra is shorter, and kidney infections are also more common in children, in pregnancy and in older people.
A weakened immune system and poorly controlled diabetes are other risk factors named by the NHS.
Diagnosis combines the story of the symptoms, a physical examination, and laboratory and imaging tests, according to the US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK).
The NHS says a GP can use a dipstick test on a urine sample to look for signs of infection.
The sample can also be sent to a laboratory, where the bacterium is identified and tested against antibiotics, and urine tests can show blood and white blood cells.
Blood tests check for serious infection.
Treatment usually starts before the laboratory results come back.
Because kidney infection is much rarer in men, men are routinely investigated further, and other causes such as kidney stones are considered when there is blood in the urine.
entries.note: NHS: men investigated; StatPearls: consider stones if haematuria

entries.sentence: Antibiotics are the main treatment, and the NHS says most people can be treated at home with antibiotic tablets or capsules.
People with a long-term health condition, or who are pregnant, may need antibiotics through a drip in hospital.
NICE guidance also sends young babies to a paediatric specialist for antibiotics into a vein, and adults who are pregnant or significantly dehydrated are among those referred to hospital.
entries.note: NICE NG111 referral points: under 3 months to paediatric specialist IV; adults pregnant or dehydrated/unable to take oral fluids

entries.sentence: The antibiotic may be changed according to the laboratory results, and the NIDDK stresses finishing the full course even when symptoms fade, because incomplete courses can promote antibiotic resistance.
When a blockage such as a stone or an enlarged prostate is the cause, a procedure or surgery may be needed to clear it.
For pain and fever, paracetamol, rest and plenty of fluids are the usual measures.
Anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen are not usually recommended because of possible effects on kidney function.
Serious complications are uncommon.
A kidney infection can lead to sepsis, which can be life threatening, and rarely to a kidney abscess or some permanent damage to kidney tissue.
NICE lists impaired kidney function, kidney failure, sepsis and preterm labour in pregnancy among the complications of acute pyelonephritis.
Most people make a full recovery when treatment starts promptly.
It may take up to 2 weeks before someone is fit enough to return to work, and older people or those with underlying conditions may take longer.
The NIDDK says symptoms that come back after treatment need prompt medical evaluation.

The NHS describes habits that help keep the bladder and urethra free of bacteria: drinking plenty of plain water, going to the toilet promptly, emptying the bladder after sex and wiping from front to back.
Treating constipation is also mentioned, as constipation can increase the chance of a bladder or kidney infection.
For people who keep getting urine infections, a GP may prescribe low-dose antibiotics.
Because most kidney infections begin as bladder infections, getting a bladder infection checked and treated is part of the picture.
entries.note: NHS: usually caused by cystitis; treat promptly

entries.sentence: The NHS says to see a GP when a fever comes with pain in the tummy, lower back or genitals that does not go away.
A GP should be contacted straight away if a child may have a kidney infection.
Ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 for a very high or very low temperature, pain in the lower tummy or back, blood in the urine, or pregnancy with these symptoms.
Call 999 or go to A&E if there is confusion or drowsiness.
Anyone whose symptoms return or persist after treatment should be reassessed by a GP.
entries.note: NIDDK: returning symptoms warrant prompt evaluation

entries.sentence: The NHS stresses that a kidney infection needs prompt treatment with antibiotics, and that without it the infection can lead to sepsis.
entries.note: NHS summary: requires prompt treatment; untreated can lead to sepsis

entries.sentence: A kidney infection is one type of urinary tract infection, the type that affects one or both kidneys.
It is often caused by cystitis, a bladder infection, spreading upwards.
It tends to cause back or side pain and fever as well as, or instead of, bladder symptoms.
The NHS describes antibiotics as the main treatment and says prompt treatment matters.
Left untreated, a kidney infection can lead to sepsis, which can be life threatening.
Anyone with symptoms should therefore contact a GP or NHS 111 rather than wait to see whether it settles.
The NHS and NICE both say anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen are not usually recommended in a kidney infection.
NICE gives concern about kidney safety as the reason.
Paracetamol is the pain and fever relief the sources mention.
The NICE committee considered paracetamol reasonable for adults, children and young people.
The NHS lists pregnancy among the reasons to seek urgent advice from a GP or NHS 111 with these symptoms.
Pregnant people may need antibiotics through a drip in hospital.
NICE lists preterm labour among the complications of acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy.
Pregnancy is one of the situations where NICE says an adult with acute pyelonephritis should be referred to hospital.
entries.note: NICE NG111 referral triggers include pregnancy

entries.sentence: Most people recover fully when treatment starts promptly.
The NHS suggests it may take up to 2 weeks before someone is fit enough to return to work.
Older people or those with underlying conditions may take longer.
Pyelonephritis
A urinary tract infection that affects one or both kidneys, usually caused by bacteria
Often a bladder infection (cystitis) that spreads upwards
Back or side pain, fever and nausea
Antibiotics, with hospital care and drip treatment for some people
Symptoms and examination, urine tests, and sometimes blood tests and imaging
